courses.title: Relational Design & Normalization
findings: The 1NF/2NF/3NF overview is useful, but normalization definitions and practical trade-offs should be presented as relational-design guidance rather than an unconditional schema recipe.
SERIAL, TIMESTAMPTZ, and PostgreSQL constraint syntax are provider-specific and should be labeled as PostgreSQL examples; equivalent identity/auto-increment behavior differs across engines.

The checklist rule that every foreign key must have an explicit ON DELETE action is a project policy, not a universal requirement; the chosen action must follow domain semantics, and CASCADE can cause unintended deletion.
The claim that composite keys with more than three columns should be avoided is an unsupported heuristic and should be reframed around key stability, access paths, and domain constraints.
The polymorphic/EAV and NULL guidance needs caveats: these patterns can be valid in constrained designs, though they carry queryability and integrity trade-offs.
actions: add engine/version scope and canonical citations
label ICIL checklist preferences separately from relational requirements
replace the fixed composite-key threshold with decision criteria
explain deletion semantics and test destructive cascades

courses.title: SQL Mastery
findings: SQL is not a single uniform implementation: the logical query-processing model is useful, but JOIN behavior, date functions, window features, NULL semantics, and syntax vary by engine.
DATE_TRUNC, the PostgreSQL-style window/CTE examples, and positional GROUP BY are provider- or dialect-sensitive and need explicit scope.
The growth example can divide by zero when the prior revenue is zero; the course should show a NULLIF or equivalent guard before presenting it as copy-ready SQL.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query in PostgreSQL, so the recommendation needs a read-only/safe-environment warning and transaction or workload caveats.
The >10K-row checklist threshold is arbitrary without a workload, plan, latency, and selectivity context.
actions: add SQL dialect and tested-version labels
qualify the logical execution-order diagram
guard the division-by-zero case
warn that EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes statements and replace row-count thresholds with measurement guidance

courses.title: Indexing & Query Optimization
findings: The opening claim that indexes are the number-one performance lever and can turn 1 ms into 30 seconds is uncited and too absolute; latency depends on workload, plan, data distribution, hardware, and contention.

The index table is PostgreSQL-specific. Hash indexes are not generally guaranteed to be faster than B-tree, and BRIN suitability should be based on physical correlation and table characteristics rather than a 10M-row threshold.
The rule to always index every foreign key is an operational heuristic, not a universal guarantee; write cost, join direction, workload, and existing indexes must be evaluated.
The statement that a function in WHERE kills an index is too broad: expression indexes, generated columns, operator classes, and planner behavior can change the outcome.
The SELECT-star/covering-index explanation confuses index-only scan eligibility with a general claim that indexes are wasted; covering indexes also have storage and write-maintenance costs.
actions: remove or source numeric performance claims
scope the index catalog and EXPLAIN syntax to a tested PostgreSQL version
replace ALWAYS and threshold rules with plan- and workload-based criteria
explain expression/partial/covering indexes and their maintenance trade-offs

courses.title: Database Migrations
findings: Expand/contract and immutable migration history are sound general patterns, but rollback is not always a safe or possible inverse after data transformation or external side effects.
The claim that ALTER TABLE changing a default locks a table for ten minutes is workload- and version-dependent and should not be stated as a universal outcome.
Adding a nullable column may avoid a table rewrite in some PostgreSQL versions and cases, but lock acquisition, indexes, constraints, and concurrent traffic still require testing.
A fixed backfill batch size of 1000 is an arbitrary starting point; batch size, throttling, retryability, idempotency, and replica impact need workload-based tuning.

The example drops and renames columns during a swap, which can break old application versions and is not a safe zero-downtime pattern without compatibility sequencing, validation, and a recovery plan.
actions: qualify lock/rewrite behavior by engine and version
distinguish rollback, roll-forward, and backup restore strategies
replace the fixed batch size with measured throttling guidance
rewrite the swap example around expand/contract compatibility and deployment sequencing
add an explicit warning that DROP COLUMN is destructive

courses.title: NoSQL Databases
findings: The SQL-versus-NoSQL decision tree is a useful orientation, but database choice cannot be reduced to data shape; access patterns, consistency, durability, operational maturity, cost, and failure modes also matter.

The CAP diagram's 'pick two of three' framing and fixed CP/AP/CA assignments are oversimplified. CAP concerns trade-offs during partitions, and behavior depends on the system, configuration, and consistency guarantees.
The MongoDB example needs a server/driver version scope and should mention deliberate access-pattern modeling, validation, and embedding-size/update trade-offs.

The Redis example uses ioredis and a Prisma-like `findUnique` call without declaring dependencies or versions; `SET` with expiration is the current general command pattern, and cache atomicity/error behavior should be explained.
Redis is not inherently only a cache and allkeys-lru is not a universal eviction policy; persistence, replication, eviction, and data-loss assumptions must be explicit.
The fixed 100 requests/minute and 1-hour TTL values are examples, not defaults, and need workload, abuse, and freshness context.
actions: replace CAP shorthand with a scoped explanation and system-specific examples
add provider, server, driver, and client-library versions
declare or remove undeclared ioredis/ORM assumptions
use current Redis expiration guidance and explain atomicity/error handling
reframe TTL, rate limits, and eviction settings as measured policy choices

courses.title: Data Modeling Patterns
findings: The pattern catalog is useful, but closure tables, event sourcing, polymorphic associations, and denormalization need workload and consistency trade-offs rather than being presented as universally superior solutions.
The recursive CTE and SERIAL examples are PostgreSQL-specific; recursion depth, cycle handling, ordering, and identity syntax need engine/version scope.
The polymorphic association example cannot enforce a normal database foreign key to multiple target tables, which conflicts with the later 'every relationship has a foreign key' checklist item.

The claim that EAV is a 'schema killer' and JSON queried data belongs in a column is too categorical; both patterns can be justified in bounded domains, with explicit validation and indexing trade-offs.
The recommendation to denormalize when reads greatly exceed writes is only a heuristic and should require measured bottlenecks, consistency strategy, and a rebuild/backfill plan.
actions: define the scope and trade-offs for each modeling pattern
add cycle, depth, and engine/version caveats to recursive examples
explain the referential-integrity limitation of polymorphic associations
replace categorical EAV/JSON language with decision criteria
require measurement and consistency planning before denormalization

courses.title: Security & Backup

sources.name: PostgreSQL continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery

findings: The layered security model is directionally sound, but network isolation is not sufficient by itself; authentication, authorization, patching, monitoring, and recovery controls need engine/provider scope.

The SQL examples contain production-looking passwords and create a SUPERUSER login. They must be replaced with inert placeholders and explicit secret-management, non-superuser, and connection/TLS caveats.

The backup pipeline is incomplete: pg_dump format determines the restore command, and `pg_restore` does not directly restore a plain SQL dump as shown. Backup consistency, encryption key management, integrity verification, and failure handling are not covered.
WAL archiving configuration is version-, filesystem-, and operationally sensitive; the example needs archive durability, command exit-status, retention, monitoring, and restore-test caveats.

The 3-2-1 rule and daily/monthly cadence are useful policy patterns but not universal requirements; RPO/RTO, data classification, immutability, ransomware recovery, and tested restores should drive the plan.

The blanket prohibition on public database ports is a strong default, but deployment-specific controls and managed-service connectivity should be described without implying VPC alone is a complete defense.
actions: replace all credential-looking examples with unmistakably inert values
remove SUPERUSER from the normal application walkthrough and document role separation
correct the pg_dump/pg_restore format example and add restore verification
scope WAL/PITR commands to a tested PostgreSQL version and operational setup
add RPO/RTO, immutable/offline backup, key-management, monitoring, and restore-drill guidance

courses.title: Core Web Vitals & Frontend Perf

sources.name: web.dev — Defining Core Web Vitals metric thresholds

findings: The LCP, INP, and CLS thresholds are aligned with current Core Web Vitals guidance, but metric definitions and thresholds are maintained guidance and should carry an access date.
The statement that poor scores equal poor SEO ranking is too broad; search ranking is multi-factor and the course should describe CWV as one signal rather than a guaranteed ranking outcome.
The field-versus-lab distinction is correct, but Lighthouse does not provide field INP; field measurement needs CrUX or RUM and lab tools use proxies such as TBT.
The checklist's universal 3G/mobile and 200KB bundle rules are useful test policies but not universal requirements; they should be framed as project budgets based on audience and measurement.
The claim that font-display and size-adjust prevent layout shift needs qualification: font metrics, fallback selection, loading behavior, and page layout determine the outcome.
actions: add source access dates and clarify CWV guidance can change
replace the SEO implication with a bounded ranking/performance caveat
distinguish field INP from lab proxies explicitly
label mobile/network and bundle limits as project-specific budgets
qualify the font metric example and test it across fallback/rendering paths

courses.title: Caching Strategies
findings: The cache-layer model is useful, but the database cache layer and provider behavior vary; query caching, materialized views, and application caches should not be presented as interchangeable.

The one-hour Redis TTL, one-year asset TTL, 1–60 minute API TTL, and 80% hit-rate rule are illustrative policy values, not generally valid defaults; freshness, privacy, invalidation cost, and workload should drive them.
The Redis example assumes a specific client/library and ORM without declaring versions or failure behavior. JSON parsing, cache errors, concurrent misses, and stale data need handling guidance.
Deleting one key on a write does not solve distributed invalidation, key fan-out, race conditions, or cache stampedes; the course needs bounded cache-aside safety guidance.
The blanket statement that POST/PUT/DELETE responses should not be cached is too broad without distinguishing HTTP cache semantics, explicit cache controls, and application-specific behavior.
actions: scope examples to declared Redis/client/ORM versions or make them pseudocode
reframe TTL and hit-rate numbers as workload-tested starting points
add cache-miss concurrency, error, invalidation, and stampede considerations
qualify HTTP method caching guidance with RFC semantics and authorization/privacy controls
add metrics beyond hit rate, including staleness, origin load, and eviction behavior

courses.title: Backend Optimization

sources.name: Node.js — Don't block the event loop

findings: The N+1 example identifies a real class of inefficiency, but eager loading is not always one query and can create large joins, duplicate rows, or over-fetching; batching and measured query plans are alternatives.
The pool max=20, 30-second idle timeout, 2-second connection timeout, and ~100ms connection overhead are environment-specific examples, not safe defaults.
The fire-and-forget queue example can lose work or hide errors if enqueueing fails, and it omits retries, idempotency, dead-letter handling, transaction/outbox coordination, and graceful shutdown.
The checklist's instruction to eliminate ALL N+1 queries is too absolute; some bounded or intentionally batched access patterns may be acceptable after measurement.
Compression choice and level depend on payloads, CPU, proxy, and content negotiation; a fixed gzip level should be presented as a test parameter.
actions: explain eager loading trade-offs and include batching/projection alternatives
label pool values as workload- and deployment-specific
replace fire-and-forget with a durable queue safety pattern
add event-loop blocking, CPU-bound work, and worker-thread boundaries
tie compression settings to benchmarked payload and CPU trade-offs

courses.title: Database Performance
findings: The course is PostgreSQL-specific but does not identify a tested PostgreSQL version, extension availability, or permissions for ALTER SYSTEM and pg_stat_statements.
The missing-index 1ms-to-30-second claim and 'fixes 30% of slow queries' claim are uncited and too absolute; plans depend on data distribution, selectivity, hardware, contention, and workload.
'Index every foreign key' and 'use cursor pagination for lists over 1000 rows' are heuristics, not universal rules; index usefulness and pagination strategy require measured access patterns.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement, and production diagnosis may need read-only safeguards, transaction strategy, BUFFERS, and representative data; this warning is absent.
Index creation, ALTER SYSTEM, logging, and pg_stat_statements have lock, overhead, permissions, and operational implications that need production-safe boundaries.
actions: add PostgreSQL version/extension/permission scope
remove or source numeric performance claims
replace universal index and pagination rules with plan/workload criteria
warn that EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes statements and show safe diagnosis options
cover index-build locking, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY trade-offs, and observability overhead

courses.title: Network & Asset Optimization
findings: The format recommendations are useful orientation, but size reductions such as 25–35% and 10x are workload-, encoder-, and content-dependent and need sourcing or softer language.
The Nginx Brotli/HTTP/3 snippets are deployment- and version-specific; the course should distinguish server configuration, CDN configuration, and browser negotiation.
HTTP/2's server push is obsolete in the modern web platform and should not appear as a current capability without an explicit historical/deprecation note.
The immutable one-year cache policy is safe only with reliable content hashing and deployment invalidation; API `private` caching also needs authorization, personalization, and privacy caveats.
The course does not cover selective resource hints; overusing preload or preconnect can compete with critical resources and harm performance.
actions: source or qualify compression and size-reduction numbers
scope Nginx/HTTP/3 snippets to tested versions and deployment roles
remove or clearly mark HTTP/2 server push as historical
tie immutable caching to verified hash/version deployment behavior
add selective preload/preconnect guidance and content-negotiation caveats

courses.title: Load Testing & Profiling
findings: The k6 scenario is a useful example, but 100 VUs, 500ms/1000ms percentile thresholds, and a 1% error target are workload-specific acceptance criteria, not general health thresholds.
The example lacks authorization, environment isolation, rate limits, test-data cleanup, third-party dependency controls, and an explicit prohibition on unapproved production load tests.
The claim that P95 spikes at 200 VUs identifies a bottleneck is too strong without accounting for arrival model, ramp schedule, saturation, coordinated omission, and downstream dependencies.
Node profiler flags and the `0x` tool are version/tooling-sensitive; generated profiles may contain sensitive code or data and need handling guidance.
The course should distinguish smoke, load, stress, spike, and soak tests and require an observable hypothesis before optimization.
actions: label VUs, percentile, and error thresholds as example SLOs
add an authorization and safe-environment load-test gate
explain traffic models, saturation, downstream limits, and result interpretation
scope profiler commands to Node/tool versions and add artifact-safety notes
add test-type selection and an explicit hypothesis/measurement workflow

courses.title: Performance Budgets & CI
findings: The budget model is sound, but fixed LCP/TBT/CLS, JS/CSS/image sizes, and a 20% improvement target are illustrative values that should be derived from a baseline, audience, route, and product goals.
TBT is a lab metric and should not be presented as a replacement for field INP; the course needs an explicit lab-versus-field mapping.
A Lighthouse CI score or assertion can be noisy across runners and browser versions; strict PR blocking needs repeated runs, variance handling, pinned tooling, and a clear policy for flaky failures.
The sample workflow omits dependency/tool version pinning, server startup/readiness, artifact retention, and whether temporary public upload is acceptable for the project's data.
The bundle-size and 10% increase limits are project policies, not universal thresholds, and should account for compression, route splitting, and intentional feature changes.
actions: derive budgets from measured baselines and label examples as project policy
distinguish TBT lab use from field INP monitoring
add repeat/variance/flakiness controls and pin Lighthouse tooling
document server readiness, artifacts, privacy, and upload configuration
make bundle thresholds route- and product-specific with an exception process

courses.title: Testing Fundamentals & Pyramid

sources.name: Martin Fowler — The Practical Test Pyramid

findings: The pyramid's qualitative cost/speed trade-off is useful, but the 70% unit, 20% integration, 10% E2E checklist is an unsupported fixed ratio; test distribution should follow risk, architecture, and feedback needs.

The statement that an inverted pyramid is a disaster is too absolute; a system may intentionally use more higher-level tests when component boundaries or domain risk require them, although cost and feedback trade-offs remain.
The test-quality table's <100ms unit and <2s integration limits are project budgets, not general definitions of a good test.

The TDD example is pedagogically useful, but TDD is a development approach rather than a requirement for every codebase or feature, and testing principles should also cover exploratory and non-functional testing.
The recommendation to run npm test before every commit assumes a project script and may create developer friction; fast local checks and full CI suites should be distinguished.
actions: replace the fixed pyramid ratio with risk- and feedback-based guidance
label speed targets as illustrative budgets
qualify TDD/BDD as context-dependent approaches
add core testing principles such as exhaustive testing being impossible and testing showing defect presence
separate fast pre-commit checks from full CI execution

courses.title: Unit & Component Testing
findings: The behavior-focused component-testing guidance aligns with Testing Library principles, but the example uses vi.fn without naming Vitest configuration, globals, or an alternative for Jest users.
The fixed ≥80% line and 100% critical-branch coverage targets are policy examples, not universal quality thresholds; coverage measures execution, not correctness or risk coverage.
The <5-second entire unit suite target is not portable across repository size, CI hardware, parallelism, or test type; it should be a measured feedback objective.

The rule 'mock external APIs, never call real services' is sound for unit tests but should distinguish unit isolation from integration/contract tests that deliberately exercise controlled real boundaries.
The one-assertion-per-test anti-pattern is too categorical; a cohesive behavior may reasonably have multiple related assertions.
actions: declare Vitest/Jest setup assumptions and versions for code examples
reframe coverage and suite-time numbers as risk-based project budgets
distinguish unit mocks from integration and contract-test boundaries
replace one-assertion language with cohesive-behavior guidance
add accessible user-facing query guidance for component tests

courses.title: Integration & API Testing
findings: The integration examples are useful, but the Supertest/ORM/database stack is implicit and should name the framework, database engine, and test-runner assumptions.

The recommendation to use transaction rollback as the preferred test-database strategy is not universal; isolation, connection pooling, background workers, DDL, and parallel tests can escape or conflict with the transaction.

The checklist requiring every endpoint to test 200, 400, 401, 403, 404, and 500 creates a fixed matrix that may be inappropriate for endpoints whose valid states differ; behavior and threat-model coverage should drive cases.

The in-memory SQLite option is not equivalent to a production PostgreSQL/MySQL/other engine and can hide dialect, locking, constraint, and query-plan differences; realistic engine validation is needed at an appropriate layer.
The course should include contract testing and API authorization cases such as broken object-level authorization, not only status-code and happy-path assertions.
actions: scope examples to declared framework, ORM, database, and runner versions
compare rollback, isolated schemas/databases, containers, and cleanup strategies
replace fixed status-code coverage with endpoint-specific behavior and threat-model cases
warn that in-memory databases are not production-engine substitutes
add contract-testing and OWASP API authorization guidance

courses.title: E2E & UI Testing
findings: The statement that Playwright dominates in 2026 and is faster/more reliable/better than Cypress or Selenium is a time-sensitive, unsupported comparative claim; tool choice depends on browser coverage, team skills, architecture, and constraints.

The selector priority incorrectly presents data-testid as universally best; Playwright guidance generally favors user-facing roles, labels, and test IDs when appropriate, with locator choice based on user contract and stability.
The payment example uses test card data and production-looking checkout behavior without explicitly requiring a sandbox, isolated test account, and third-party payment mocking or test mode.
Retries can conceal flakiness if treated as a fix; the course needs distinction between retry diagnostics, quarantine policy, and root-cause remediation.
Cached storageState can leak mutable account state between workers or tests; account isolation, expiry, and cleanup requirements are missing.
actions: replace the dated tool dominance claim with criteria-based tool selection
prioritize accessible/user-facing locators and scope test IDs appropriately
mark payment flows as sandbox-only with isolated data and third-party boundaries
treat retries as diagnostic/safety mechanisms, not flaky-test fixes
add worker-safe authentication state, account isolation, and teardown guidance

courses.title: Performance & Load Testing
findings: Load testing is valuable, but the claim that it is the only way to catch capacity issues before users do is too absolute; modeling, profiling, observability, and controlled experiments also contribute.
The 50 VUs, P95<500ms, and error-rate<1% values are illustrative acceptance criteria, not general health thresholds; targets should derive from workload, geography, endpoint mix, and SLOs.
The recommendation to load test before every major release needs authorization, environment isolation, downstream dependency controls, data cleanup, rate-limit protection, and cost safeguards.
The example targets a live-looking API URL and lacks explicit prohibition against unapproved production testing or third-party side effects.
The course should distinguish open/closed traffic models, test repetition, warm-up, confidence/variance, and representative workload design rather than treating one scenario as capacity evidence.
actions: label VU, percentile, and error thresholds as example SLOs
add an explicit authorization and isolated-environment load-test gate
protect downstream services and test data from side effects
add workload-model, warm-up, repetition, variance, and result-interpretation guidance
replace the claim that load testing is the only capacity method with a broader measurement workflow

courses.title: CI/CD Test Automation
findings: The workflow is a useful template, but action versions, Node/runtime behavior, permissions, caching, artifact retention, and runner images are version- and repository-policy-sensitive.
The statement that tests only run on developer machines are useless is too absolute; local checks are valuable, while CI provides reproducibility and shared enforcement.
The example contains a TODO inside test.skip and was correctly flagged by the structural scanner as a placeholder; skipped tests need an owner, issue reference, expiry/review policy, and visibility.
Running the full lint/typecheck/unit/E2E suite on every push may be costly; path filters, pull-request tiers, nightly suites, matrix builds, and protected-branch gates should be considered.
Retries, sharding, and uploaded artifacts need safeguards against masking failures, nondeterministic ordering, secret leakage, and excessive CI cost.
actions: pin and periodically review action/runtime versions and permissions
replace the TODO/skip example with an explicit quarantine policy and tracking reference
distinguish local feedback from CI enforcement
add cost-aware pipeline tiers, path filters, matrix/shard strategy, and protected gates
document retry, artifact privacy, retention, and failure-triage rules

courses.title: Quality Metrics & Strategy
findings: Coverage, mutation, flakiness, and escaped-bug metrics can inform quality, but the table's universal targets (80%, 75%, 60%, <1%, <10%) are unsupported without product and risk context.

The opening claim that quality is measurable is incomplete; quantitative signals complement qualitative review, exploratory testing, usability, security, and production evidence rather than replacing them.
Running Stryker monthly across an entire codebase may be expensive and should be scoped to critical modules, changed code, scheduled jobs, or sampled campaigns.
Flakiness and escape-rate denominators, time windows, test retries, severity weighting, and detection boundaries are not defined, so values cannot yet be compared reliably.
The course should include DORA delivery/stability metrics carefully and warn against Goodhart effects such as adding meaningless assertions to hit coverage targets.
actions: replace universal thresholds with risk-based baselines and trend interpretation
define metric denominators, windows, severity, and retry treatment
scope mutation testing by risk, changed code, or scheduled budget
add qualitative/exploratory/security/production evidence to the quality strategy
add Goodhart and metric-gaming safeguards plus DORA metric context
